citations.quote: Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

If $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ are IID real random variables and $\mathbb E|X_1|<\infty$, then, with $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$ and $\mu=\mathbb EX_1$,
$$\mathbb E|S_n/n-\mu|\longrightarrow0.$$
Consequently $S_n/n\to\mu$ in probability.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Fix integers $d,n\ge1$ and observed vectors $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$, with the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Their empirical law is the set function
$$P_n(A)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n 1\{x_i\in A\},\qquad A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d).$$

Let $\mathsf I_n=\{\omega:[n]\to[n]\}$ be the finite set of index vectors. By [[thm-cardinality-of-a-set-of-functions]], it has $n^n$ elements. Give each index vector mass $n^{-n}$; the weights sum to one, so this is a finite probability space in the sense of [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]. For $j=1,\ldots,n$, let $I_j(\omega)=\omega(j)$ and put $X_j^*(\omega)=x_{I_j(\omega)}$. The **ideal size-$n$ empirical bootstrap law conditional on the data** is the pushforward of this finite uniform law under
$\omega\longmapsto (x_{\omega(1)},\ldots,x_{\omega(n)}).$
Thus conditional probabilities are finite averages over the $n^n$ index tuples. The empirical law is a probability measure, and the bootstrap coordinates are conditionally IID with that law, by the well-definedness results listed in justified_by.

For random observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, write $\bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_iX_i$ coordinatewise, so each coordinate is the scalar sample mean in [[def-partial-sums-and-sample-means]]. Write $P_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{X_i}$, using the Dirac measure [[def-dirac-measure]], and let $\bar X_n^*$ be the bootstrap mean. If $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is Borel ([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]), then
$$\hat\theta_n=g(\bar X_n),\qquad \hat\theta_n^*=g(\bar X_n^*).$$
When $X_i$ are IID ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]) with finite second moment, write $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_{1j}$ and $\Sigma_{jk}=\mathbb E[(X_{1j}-\mu_j)(X_{1k}-\mu_k)]$ ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]), and set $\theta=g(\mu)$. The functions of the data above are Borel statistics and estimators in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; coordinatewise arithmetic preserves measurability ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]). No bootstrap validity or interval coverage is part of this definition. For $n\ge2$, the delete-one mean and plug-in statistic are
$$\bar X_{n,(-i)}=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{j\ne i}X_j,\qquad \hat\theta_{n,(-i)}=g(\bar X_{n,(-i)}).$$

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $a=(a_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ take values in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$ ([[def-extended-reals]]). Its **partial sums** are the unique sequence $(s_n)$ in $[0,+\infty]$ satisfying

$$s_0=0,\qquad s_{n+1}=s_n+a_n.$$

To apply [[thm-recursion]] with a fixed successor function, use the state space $\mathbb N\times[0,+\infty]$ and the self-map $T(n,s)=(n+1,s+a_n)$, starting from $(0,0)$. Recursion gives a unique state sequence; induction makes its first coordinate $n$, and its second coordinates are exactly the unique $(s_n)$ satisfying the displayed recurrence. Addition of two nonnegative extended reals is always defined, including when either is $+\infty$. The sequence $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing, and its **nonnegative extended sum** is

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k:=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}s_n\in[0,+\infty],$$

whose existence follows from completeness of the extended real line ([[lem-extended-reals-complete]]). More generally, for $m\in\mathbb N$,

$$\sum_{k\ge m}a_k:=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_{m+j}.$$

Finite sums use the same recursion: $\sum_{k<n}a_k=s_n$, so the empty sum at $n=0$ is $0$. A double sum such as $\sum_i\sum_j a_{ij}$ means that the inner nonnegative extended sum is formed first and the resulting nonnegative extended sequence is then summed.

Let $(A_k)_{k\ge1}$ be pairwise disjoint Borel sets. For each fixed $i$, at most one indicator $1\{x_i\in A_k\}$ is nonzero. Therefore $P_n\!\left(\bigcup_{k\ge1}A_k\right)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k\ge1}1\{x_i\in A_k\} =\sum_{k\ge1}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n1\{x_i\in A_k\} =\sum_{k\ge1}P_n(A_k).$ The interchange is between a finite sum and a nonnegative series; by [F4] both are the supremum of the corresponding finite partial sums, so finite distributivity gives the equality.
Steps 1.1 and 1.2 verify the empty-set and countable-additivity clauses in [F2], and step 1.1 gives total mass one. Thus [F3] makes $P_n$ a probability measure.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

derivations.claim: On $E_n$, define $\varphi_i(t)=g(\bar X_n-t(X_i-\bar X_n)/(n-1))$ for $0\le t\le1$. It is continuous on $[0,1]$ and differentiable on $(0,1)$ by [F5], with derivative $-(n-1)^{-1}\nabla g(\bar X_n-t(X_i-\bar X_n)/(n-1))^T(X_i-\bar X_n)$. By [F4] there is $\tau_i\in(0,1)$ at which this derivative equals $\varphi_i(1)-\varphi_i(0)$. On every outcome define the measurable algebraic remainder $e_{n,i}:=\hat\theta_{n,(-i)}-\hat\theta_n+a^T(X_i-\bar X_n)/(n-1)$. On $E_n$ the mean-value identity expresses this remainder as $-\frac{(\nabla g(\bar X_n-\tau_i(X_i-\bar X_n)/(n-1))-a)^T(X_i-\bar X_n)}{n-1}$, so $|e_{n,i}|\le\omega_n\|X_i-\bar X_n\|/(n-1)$. The points $\tau_i$ are used only for this pointwise identity and bound; no measurable selection is needed. Since $\mathbb P(E_n)\to1$, the expansion with the stated bound holds with probability tending to one.

The algebraic definition of $e_{n,i}$ gives $p_{n,i}=\hat\theta_n+a^T(X_i-\bar X_n)-(n-1)e_{n,i}$. On $E_n$, the bound in step 2.1 makes the average squared error in the statement at most $\omega_n^2\,\frac1n\sum_i\|X_i-\bar X_n\|^2,$ which tends to zero in probability by step 1.1. Since $\mathbb P(E_n^c)\to0$, the stated convergence in probability follows.

The algebraic definition of $e_{n,i}$ gives, after averaging over $i$ and using $\sum_i(X_i-\bar X_n)=0$, $$nV_{J,n}=\frac1{n-1}\sum_i\left(a^T(X_i-\bar X_n)-(n-1)(e_{n,i}-\bar e_n)\right)^2,$$ where $\bar e_n=n^{-1}\sum_ie_{n,i}$. The leading quadratic term is $\frac1{n-1}\sum_i\{a^T(X_i-\bar X_n)\}^2=\frac n{n-1}a^T\widehat\Sigma_n a\longrightarrow a^T\Sigma a$ by [F1]. On $E_n$, the normalized squared error term is bounded by $(n-1)\sum_i(e_{n,i}-\bar e_n)^2\le(n-1)\sum_i e_{n,i}^2\le\omega_n^2\frac1{n-1}\sum_i\|X_i-\bar X_n\|^2\longrightarrow0.$ If $\psi_i=a^T(X_i-\bar X_n)$ and $r_i=(n-1)(e_{n,i}-\bar e_n)$, then on $E_n$ the absolute cross term is at most $2\sqrt{\left(\frac1{n-1}\sum_i\psi_i^2\right)\left(\frac1{n-1}\sum_i r_i^2\right)},$ which tends to zero because the first factor converges to the finite $a^T\Sigma a$ and the second to zero. Since $\mathbb P(E_n^c)\to0$, these bounds prove the jackknife variance limit in probability.

Fix integers $d,n\ge1$ and observed vectors $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$, with the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Their empirical law is the set function
$$P_n(A)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n 1\{x_i\in A\},\qquad A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d).$$

Let $\mathsf I_n=\{\omega:[n]\to[n]\}$ be the finite set of index vectors. By [[thm-cardinality-of-a-set-of-functions]], it has $n^n$ elements. Give each index vector mass $n^{-n}$; the weights sum to one, so this is a finite probability space in the sense of [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]. For $j=1,\ldots,n$, let $I_j(\omega)=\omega(j)$ and put $X_j^*(\omega)=x_{I_j(\omega)}$. The **ideal size-$n$ empirical bootstrap law conditional on the data** is the pushforward of this finite uniform law under
$\omega\longmapsto (x_{\omega(1)},\ldots,x_{\omega(n)}).$
Thus conditional probabilities are finite averages over the $n^n$ index tuples. The empirical law is a probability measure, and the bootstrap coordinates are conditionally IID with that law, by the well-definedness results listed in justified_by.

For random observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, write $\bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_iX_i$ coordinatewise, so each coordinate is the scalar sample mean in [[def-partial-sums-and-sample-means]]. Write $P_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{X_i}$, using the Dirac measure [[def-dirac-measure]], and let $\bar X_n^*$ be the bootstrap mean. If $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is Borel ([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]), then
$$\hat\theta_n=g(\bar X_n),\qquad \hat\theta_n^*=g(\bar X_n^*).$$
When $X_i$ are IID ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]) with finite second moment, write $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_{1j}$ and $\Sigma_{jk}=\mathbb E[(X_{1j}-\mu_j)(X_{1k}-\mu_k)]$ ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]), and set $\theta=g(\mu)$. The functions of the data above are Borel statistics and estimators in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; coordinatewise arithmetic preserves measurability ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]). No bootstrap validity or interval coverage is part of this definition. For $n\ge2$, the delete-one mean and plug-in statistic are
$$\bar X_{n,(-i)}=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{j\ne i}X_j,\qquad \hat\theta_{n,(-i)}=g(\bar X_{n,(-i)}).$$

For any $n\ge1$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$, the set function
$$P_n(A)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n1\{x_i\in A\},\qquad A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d),$$
is a probability measure.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

derivations.claim: For subsets $C_1,\ldots,C_n\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$, the product-uniform index law gives $\mathbb P^*(I_1\in C_1,\ldots,I_n\in C_n)=\frac{\prod_{j=1}^n|C_j|}{n^n} =\prod_{j=1}^n\frac{|C_j|}{n}.$ Thus the coordinate indices are independent and each is uniform on $\{1,\ldots,n\}$.

For each $j$, the map $i\mapsto x_i$ from the finite discrete index set to $\mathbb R^d$ is measurable, and its pushforward of the uniform law assigns $A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ mass $n^{-1}\sum_i1\{x_i\in A\}=P_n(A)$. Applying [F3] to the independent indices shows the values $X_j^*=x_{I_j}$ are independent; their common law is $P_n$, which is a probability law by [F2].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The functions of the data above are Borel statistics and estimators in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; coordinatewise arithmetic preserves measurability ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]). $$\bar X_{n,(-i)}=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{j\ne i}X_j,\qquad \hat\theta_{n,(-i)}=g(\bar X_{n,(-i)}).$$
For fixed data $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$, the coordinates of the finite-index bootstrap sample in [[def-iid-empirical-bootstrap-sample]] are independent and each has law $P_n$.

Let $d\ge1$ be finite and let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$. Put $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_{1j}$ and $\Sigma_{jk}=\mathbb E[(X_{1j}-\mu_j)(X_{1k}-\mu_k)]$, the coordinate covariance entries from [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Define
$$\bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i,\qquad \widehat\Sigma_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X_n)(X_i-\bar X_n)^T.$$
Then $\bar X_n\to\mu$ in probability and every entry of $\widehat\Sigma_n$ converges in probability to the corresponding entry of $\Sigma$.

For each integer $n\ge1$, let $k_n\ge1$ be a finite integer and let $X_{n,1},\ldots,X_{n,k_n}$ be integrable real random variables on a probability space $(\Omega_n,\mathcal F_n,\mathbb P_n)$. The family is a **centered triangular array** when $\mathbb E_nX_{n,k}=0$ for every admissible pair $(n,k)$. It is **row-wise independent** when, for each fixed n and all Borel sets $B_1,\ldots,B_{k_n}$, $$\mathbb P_n\!\left(\bigcap_{k=1}^{k_n}\{X_{n,k}\in B_k\}\right)=\prod_{k=1}^{k_n}\mathbb P_n(X_{n,k}\in B_k).$$ Taking unused $B_k$ equal to the real line gives the same factorization for each subfamily; by [[thm-rectangle-criterion-for-independent-random-elements]], this is exactly independence in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Random variables and integrability have the meanings in [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] and [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. There is no independence requirement between different rows. The spaces may differ with n; assertions about row sums compare their laws. A single-entry row is independent automatically, and deterministic zero entries are allowed. Empty rows are excluded by $k_n\ge1$. This definition makes no existence or choice assumption.

For a centered triangular array as in [[def-row-wise-independent-centered-triangular-array]], suppose every entry has finite second moment. Write $$v_{n,k}=\mathbb E_nX_{n,k}^2=\operatorname{Var}_n(X_{n,k}),\qquad s_n^2=\sum_{k=1}^{k_n}v_{n,k}.$$ Variance is defined in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Every term is finite and nonnegative, so the finite sum and its nonnegative square root s_n exist. Whenever $s_n>0$, define $$L_n(\varepsilon)=s_n^{-2}\sum_{k=1}^{k_n}\mathbb E_n\!\left[X_{n,k}^2\mathbf1_{\{|X_{n,k}|>\varepsilon s_n\}}\right]\quad(\varepsilon>0).$$ The **Lindeberg condition** is $L_n(\varepsilon)\to0$ for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, with $s_n>0$ for all n under consideration. The event is measurable because absolute value is continuous and the entries are measurable; products are measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]. Its nonnegative integrand is bounded by $X_{n,k}^2$, so its expectation exists and is finite by [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]] and [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. In particular $0\le L_n(\varepsilon)\le1$.

For $Y_{n,k}=X_{n,k}/s_n$, scalar homogeneity gives $\sum_k\mathbb E_nY_{n,k}^2=1$. The equality $|Y_{n,k}|>\varepsilon\Longleftrightarrow |X_{n,k}|>\varepsilon s_n$ gives $$L_n(\varepsilon)=\sum_k\mathbb E_n[Y_{n,k}^2\mathbf1_{\{|Y_{n,k}|>\varepsilon\}}].$$ Thus the normalized and unnormalized conditions are exactly equivalent, not merely asymptotic. The cutoff uses strict inequality; equality at the threshold is excluded. A zero-variance row is allowed in the initial variance definition, but its normalization and Lindeberg expression above are undefined. No independence or choice is needed to define these quantities.
Assume AC. If a centered row-wise independent triangular array has finite second moments, $s_n>0$ and the Lindeberg condition, then $$s_n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{k_n}X_{n,k}\Rightarrow N(0,1).$$

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$, write $X_n\Rightarrow X$, or
$X_n\to X$ **in distribution**, when
$$F_{X_n}(x)\longrightarrow F_X(x)$$
at every continuity point $x$ of $F_X$. Here $F_X$ is the CDF from
[[def-cumulative-distribution-function-of-a-random-variable]] and continuity
points are those of [[def-atom-and-continuity-point-of-a-law]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Phi(x)=P(Z\le x)$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Then $\Phi$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$, with $\lim_{x\to-\infty}\Phi(x)=0$ and $\lim_{x\to+\infty}\Phi(x)=1$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse ([[def-field]]). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
[[thm-of-archimedean]] on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

Let $n,d\ge1$, let $(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ be a measurable $(\mathbb R^d)^n$-valued random vector, and fix $a\in\mathbb R^d$. For each finite index tuple $\omega=(i_1,\ldots,i_n)\in\mathsf I_n=\{1,\ldots,n\}^n$, define the projected centered bootstrap-mean value
$$R_{n,\omega}=\sqrt n\,a^T\!\left(\frac1n\sum_{\ell=1}^n X_{i_\ell}-\bar X_n\right),\qquad \bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.$$
The finite-index conditional bootstrap CDF is
$$F_n^*(t)=n^{-n}\sum_{\omega\in\mathsf I_n}1\{R_{n,\omega}\le t\}.$$
For every fixed continuous cumulative distribution function $G:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$, the supremum
$$D_n=\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}|F_n^*(t)-G(t)|$$
is a measurable real random variable.
If $X_n\to X$ almost surely, then $X_n\to X$ in probability.

derivations.claim: Put $Y_i=a^T(X_i-\mu)$ and $\bar Y_n=n^{-1}\sum_iY_i$. Its variance is $\sigma^2$. By [F2], the empirical variance $s_n^2=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\bar Y_n)^2=a^T\widehat\Sigma_n a$ converges in probability to $\sigma^2>0$, while $\bar Y_n\to0$ in probability and $n^{-1}\sum_iY_i^2\to\sigma^2$ in probability.

For $t>0$, define the unnormalized empirical tail quantity $T_n(t)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\bar Y_n)^2\,1\{|Y_i-\bar Y_n|>t\sqrt n\}.$ On $|\bar Y_n|\le t\sqrt n/2$, the indicator implies $|Y_i|>t\sqrt n/2$, and $T_n(t)\le 2\,\frac1n\sum_iY_i^2\,1\{|Y_i|>t\sqrt n/2\} +2\bar Y_n^2\,\frac1n\sum_i1\{|Y_i|>t\sqrt n/2\}.$ The expectation of the first term tends to zero by [F7], so [F8] makes it converge to zero in probability. The second empirical tail fraction is at most $4(t^2n)^{-1}(n^{-1}\sum_iY_i^2)$; hence its product with $2\bar Y_n^2$ tends to zero in probability by [F2]. The complement event has probability tending to zero by [F2], so $T_n(t)\to0$ in probability for every $t>0$.

Conditionally on the data, the row variables $Z_{n\ell}^*=n^{-1/2}a^T(X_\ell^*-\bar X_n)$, $1\le\ell\le n$, are independent and centered by [F1]. They are finite conditional rows of the type in [F3], with total variance $s_n^2$. By [F4], when $s_n>0$ their normalized Lindeberg quantity at threshold $\varepsilon>0$ is $s_n^{-2}T_n(\varepsilon s_n)$. On $s_n\ge\sigma/2$, this is at most $4\sigma^{-2}T_n(\varepsilon\sigma/2)$, which tends to zero in probability by step 1.2; also $s_n^2\to\sigma^2$ in probability by [F2].

Take any subsequence, indexed $(n_k)_{k\ge1}$. Recursively, after $k_0=0$, let $k_j$ be the least integer $k>k_{j-1}$ for which $\mathbb P(|s_{n_k}^2-\sigma^2|>1/j)+\sum_{r=1}^j\mathbb P(T_{n_k}(1/r)>1/j)<2^{-j}$. For fixed $j$, each of these finitely many probabilities tends to zero as $k\to\infty$ by [F2] and step 1.2, so the qualifying set is nonempty; [F12] gives its least index.

Let $E_j$ be the union of the variance-deviation event and the $j$ tail events at index $k_j$. By [F9], $\mathbb P(E_j)<2^{-j}$ and $\mathbb P(\bigcup_{j\ge m}E_j)\le\sum_{j\ge m}2^{-j}=2^{1-m}$. The event that infinitely many $E_j$ occur is contained in every such tail union, so its probability is zero. Off this null event, $s_{n_{k_j}}^2\to\sigma^2$ and, for every fixed $r\ge1$, $T_{n_{k_j}}(1/r)\to0$. For any $t>0$, choose $r$ with $1/r<t$ by [F13]; since $T_n$ is nonincreasing, $0\le T_{n_{k_j}}(t)\le T_{n_{k_j}}(1/r)\to0$.

Along almost every selected data path, $s_{n_{k_j}}\to\sigma>0$, and for every $\varepsilon>0$ the Lindeberg quantity is eventually bounded by $4\sigma^{-2}T_{n_{k_j}}(\varepsilon\sigma/2)\to0$. Thus the deterministic conditional rows satisfy [F5], giving $\sum_{\ell=1}^{n_{k_j}}Z_{n_{k_j},\ell}^*/s_{n_{k_j}}\Rightarrow N(0,1)$. Every starting subsequence has a further subsequence with this almost-sure conditional convergence.

Along each data sequence from step 4.1, put $m_j=n_{k_j}$ and let $H_j$ be the conditional CDF of $\sum_{\ell=1}^{m_j}Z_{m_j,\ell}^*/s_{m_j}$, discarding finitely many rows before $s_{m_j}>0$. By [F6], $H_j(t)\to\Phi(t)$ for every real $t$. Fix $x\in\mathbb R$ and $h>0$. Since $s_{m_j}\to\sigma>0$, eventually $x/\sigma-h\le x/s_{m_j}\le x/\sigma+h$, so monotonicity gives $H_j(x/\sigma-h)\le F_{m_j}^*(x)=H_j(x/s_{m_j})\le H_j(x/\sigma+h)$. Letting $j\to\infty$ and then $h\downarrow0$, continuity in [F10] yields $F_{m_j}^*(x)\to\Phi(x/\sigma)=\Phi_\sigma(x)$. To make this uniform, fix $\eta>0$, choose $R$ with $\Phi_\sigma(-R)<\eta$ and $1-\Phi_\sigma(R)<\eta$, and partition $[-R,R]$ into finitely many intervals on which $\Phi_\sigma$ varies by less than $\eta$, using [F11]. Monotonicity of each conditional CDF bounds its error between grid points by the endpoint errors plus $\eta$; outside $[-R,R]$ the two tail probabilities add at most $2\eta$ plus endpoint errors. The maximum grid error tends to zero, and then $\eta\downarrow0$ proves almost-sure uniform CDF convergence along the selected subsequence. Since $D_n$ is measurable by [F14], this is almost-sure convergence of real random variables.

If $D_n$ did not converge to zero in probability, there would be $\delta,\varepsilon>0$ and a subsequence on which $\mathbb P(D_n>\delta)\ge\varepsilon$. Applying the subsequence construction in step 2.2 and its consequences in steps 3.1–5.1 gives a further subsequence with $D_n\to0$ almost surely by step 5.1. By [F15], this is convergence in probability, contradicting the lower bound.

Statement: Assumption A1: AC is explicit and is used through the Lindeberg-Feller theorem; the bootstrap index space itself is finite.

boundaries.reason: Statement proves uniform conditional Gaussian CDF convergence with finite second moment and strictly positive projected variance. Steps 4.1–6.1 use conditional Lindeberg rows and subsequences to establish the sufficient implication.

Statement does not recover finite second moments or positive variance from validity of an arbitrary bootstrap approximation. The positive variance specifically licenses the normalization at step 2.1; necessity is not claimed.

risk_review.notes: Independently read all eight proof steps and all twenty direct prerequisite statements, including the full finite-index IID proof. Finite second moment controls empirical projected tails by dominated convergence and Markov. The least-index recursion simultaneously selects variance and cutoffs 1/r; summable bad-event bounds give pathwise convergence for every threshold by monotonicity. Positive limiting variance makes normalization legal after finitely many rows, and Lindeberg-Feller allows varying finite row spaces. Deterministic scaling gives the unnormalized normal limit; continuity, tail truncation and a finite grid give uniform CDF convergence. The finite-supremum lemma supplies measurable D_n. Step 6.1 correctly uses 2.2 and 3.1-5.1, and the subsequence contradiction proves convergence in probability. AC is explicitly inherited from LF and normal suppliers; the least-index selection itself uses no AC. Washington ch8b §4 Theorem 4.1 and full proof, PDF p14, were independently read as source context. Degenerate data rows can occur for small n; sigma^2>0 ensures eventual positivity on each selected path.

Put $H_n^*=\sqrt n(\bar X_n^*-\bar X_n)$ and $V_n^*=a^TH_n^*$. By [F4], the conditional CDF of $V_n^*$ converges uniformly in probability to $\Phi_\sigma$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Phi(x)=P(Z\le x)$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Then $\Phi$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$, with $\lim_{x\to-\infty}\Phi(x)=0$ and $\lim_{x\to+\infty}\Phi(x)=1$.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $Z_n=\sqrt n\,\bar X_n\Rightarrow Z$ with $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Since absolute value is continuous, [F3] gives $\sqrt n|\bar X_n|\Rightarrow |Z|$. The limiting CDF of $|Z|$ is continuous at $0$ and equals $\mathbb P(|Z|\le0)=0$.

Let $V_n^*=\sqrt n(\bar X_n^*-\bar X_n)$. Its conditional CDF $F_n^*$ satisfies $D_n:=\sup_t|F_n^*(t)-\Phi(t)|\to0$ in probability by [F1]. The bootstrap root for $g(x)=|x|$ is $R_n^*=\sqrt n(|\bar X_n^*|-|\bar X_n|)=|Z_n+V_n^*|-|Z_n|.$ For fixed data value $Z_n=z\ge0$, the event $R_n^*\le0$ is $-2z\le V_n^*\le0$; for $z<0$, it is $0\le V_n^*\le-2z$.

For any interval $[u,v]$, the difference between its conditional bootstrap probability and its standard normal probability is at most $2D_n$: use $F_n^*(v)-F_n^*(u-)$ and take left limits in the uniform CDF bound, using continuity of $\Phi$. Therefore $Q_n:=\mathbb P^*(R_n^*\le0\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n)=\Phi(2|Z_n|)-\frac12+o_{\mathbb P}(1).$ Indeed, the normal mass of either interval in step 1.2 is $\Phi(2|z|)-1/2$. By [F3] and [F4], $Q_n\Rightarrow \Phi(2|Z|)-1/2$. This limit is positive with positive probability because $\mathbb P(|Z|\ge1)>0$ and [F5] gives $\Phi(2)-1/2>0$. Thus $Q_n$ does not converge in probability to zero.

If the conditional bootstrap law consistently estimated the sampling law of $\sqrt n|\bar X_n|$, its conditional CDF at the continuity point $0$ would converge in probability to the sampling limit CDF there, namely zero by step 1.1 and [F5]. Step 2.1 contradicts this. The failure occurs because $g(x)=|x|$ is not differentiable at the true mean $0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix integers $d,n\ge1$ and observed vectors $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$, with the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Their empirical law is the set function
$$P_n(A)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n 1\{x_i\in A\},\qquad A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d).$$

Let $\mathsf I_n=\{\omega:[n]\to[n]\}$ be the finite set of index vectors. By [[thm-cardinality-of-a-set-of-functions]], it has $n^n$ elements. Give each index vector mass $n^{-n}$; the weights sum to one, so this is a finite probability space in the sense of [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]. For $j=1,\ldots,n$, let $I_j(\omega)=\omega(j)$ and put $X_j^*(\omega)=x_{I_j(\omega)}$. The **ideal size-$n$ empirical bootstrap law conditional on the data** is the pushforward of this finite uniform law under
$\omega\longmapsto (x_{\omega(1)},\ldots,x_{\omega(n)}).$
Thus conditional probabilities are finite averages over the $n^n$ index tuples. The empirical law is a probability measure, and the bootstrap coordinates are conditionally IID with that law, by the well-definedness results listed in justified_by.

For random observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, write $\bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_iX_i$ coordinatewise, so each coordinate is the scalar sample mean in [[def-partial-sums-and-sample-means]]. Write $P_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{X_i}$, using the Dirac measure [[def-dirac-measure]], and let $\bar X_n^*$ be the bootstrap mean. If $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is Borel ([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]), then
$$\hat\theta_n=g(\bar X_n),\qquad \hat\theta_n^*=g(\bar X_n^*).$$
When $X_i$ are IID ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]) with finite second moment, write $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_{1j}$ and $\Sigma_{jk}=\mathbb E[(X_{1j}-\mu_j)(X_{1k}-\mu_k)]$ ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]), and set $\theta=g(\mu)$. The functions of the data above are Borel statistics and estimators in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; coordinatewise arithmetic preserves measurability ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]). No bootstrap validity or interval coverage is part of this definition. For $n\ge2$, the delete-one mean and plug-in statistic are
$$\bar X_{n,(-i)}=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{j\ne i}X_j,\qquad \hat\theta_{n,(-i)}=g(\bar X_{n,(-i)}).$$

Assume AC. Let $X_i$ be IID $\mathbb R^d$-valued vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean $\mu$, and covariance $\Sigma$. Let $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be Borel and Fréchet differentiable at $\mu$, with derivative $a^T$, and assume
$$0<\sigma^2:=a^T\Sigma a<\infty.$$
Set $\theta=g(\mu)$, $\hat\theta_n=g(\bar X_n)$, and $\hat\theta_n^*=g(\bar X_n^*)$ for the finite-index empirical bootstrap in [[def-iid-empirical-bootstrap-sample]]. Then
$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2),$$
and, for every fixed $x\in\mathbb R$,
$$\mathbb P^*\!\left(\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n^*-\hat\theta_n)\le x\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n\right)\longrightarrow\Phi_\sigma(x)\quad\text{in probability},$$
where $\Phi_\sigma$ is the CDF of $N(0,\sigma^2)$. Thus the ideal conditional bootstrap law and the sampling law have the same first-order limit with the stated centering and $\sqrt n$ scaling. This theorem does not imply coverage of any interval algorithm.

derivations.claim: Here $g(x)=x$ is Borel and differentiable everywhere with derivative $a=1$. Thus $a^T\Sigma a=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)=\sigma^2\in(0,\infty)$, so all assumptions of [F2] hold.

Since $\hat\theta_n=\bar X_n$ and $\hat\theta_n^*=\bar X_n^*$ by [F1], [F2] gives $\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2)$ and the conditional law of $\sqrt n(\bar X_n^*-\bar X_n)$ converges weakly in probability to the same normal law. This is first-order distributional validity only.

Let $A$ and $B$ be finite sets and write

$$A^{B} := \{\, f : f \text{ is a function } B \to A \,\}.$$

Then $A^{B}$ is finite and $\lvert A^{B}\rvert = \lvert A\rvert^{\lvert B\rvert}$,
the power being the $\mathbb{N}$-valued exponentiation of [[def-nat-power]].

Both degenerate cases are covered and neither is a stipulation. If
$B = \varnothing$ there is exactly one function $B \to A$, the empty function, so
$\lvert A^{\varnothing}\rvert = 1 = \lvert A\rvert^{0}$ **even when
$A = \varnothing$**. If $A = \varnothing$ and $B \ne \varnothing$ there is no
function at all, so $\lvert A^{B}\rvert = 0 = 0^{\lvert B\rvert}$ with
$\lvert B\rvert \ge 1$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let $E \subseteq X$. The
indicator function

$$\mathbf{1}_E(x) := \begin{cases} 1, & x \in E,\\ 0, & x \notin E \end{cases}$$

is measurable as a map $X \to \mathbb{R}$ if and only if $E \in \mathcal{A}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

Let $X$ be a real random variable. Its **cumulative distribution function** is
the function
$$F_X:\mathbb R\to[0,1],\qquad F_X(x):=\mathbb P(X\le x)=\mathbb P_X((-\infty,x]).$$

The second expression is the same quantity written in terms of the law
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] of $X$.

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

derivations.claim: Fix an outcome and let $u_1<\cdots<u_m$ be the distinct values among the finite list $(R_{n,\omega})_{\omega\in\mathsf I_n}$. Write $F_n^*(u_j^-)=n^{-n}\#\{\eta:R_{n,\eta}<u_j\}$. On $[u_j,u_{j+1})$, $F_n^*$ is constant at $F_n^*(u_j)$ and $G$ is nondecreasing, so the absolute difference is bounded by the larger of its two endpoint errors, $|F_n^*(u_j)-G(u_j)|$ and $|F_n^*(u_{j+1}^-)-G(u_{j+1})|$. For $t<u_1$, the error is at most $|F_n^*(u_1^-)-G(u_1)|$; for $t\ge u_m$, it is at most $|F_n^*(u_m)-G(u_m)|$. Each left-limit error is approached as $t\uparrow u_j$, and each right-value error occurs at $u_j$. Therefore $D_n=\max_{\omega\in\mathsf I_n}\max\{|F_n^*(R_{n,\omega})-G(R_{n,\omega})|,\ |F_n^*(R_{n,\omega}^-)-G(R_{n,\omega})|\}$, where $F_n^*(r^-)=n^{-n}\#\{\eta:R_{n,\eta}<r\}$.

For each fixed tuple $\omega$, $R_{n,\omega}$ is a finite linear combination of measurable coordinates, hence measurable by [F2]. Thus each comparison event $\{R_{n,\eta}\le R_{n,\omega}\}$ or $\{R_{n,\eta}<R_{n,\omega}\}$ is measurable by applying [F2] to the measurable difference and its Borel half-line. Consequently $F_n^*(R_{n,\omega})$ and $F_n^*(R_{n,\omega}^-)$ are measurable finite sums; $G(R_{n,\omega})$ is measurable by [F4]. The finite maximum in step 1.1 is measurable by [F2], so $D_n$ is measurable.
